sentences.text: Despite being known only from fragmentary remains, Argentinosaurus is estimated to have been 30 to 35 meters long and weighed 65 to 80 tonnes.
A reconstructed dorsal vertebra of Argentinosaurus is 159 cm tall and 129 cm wide.
The complete femur assigned to Argentinosaurus is 2.5 meters long.
Bonaparte and Coria described Argentinosaurus in 1993 and noted its ribs were hollow.
The genus Argentinosaurus was named by Bonaparte and Coria in 1993.
Argentinosaurus is estimated to have measured 31 to 37 meters in length and weighed 51 to 77 tonnes, making it a strong contender for the title of the largest land animal ever known.
Approximately 70% of the Argentinosaurus skeleton has been found, providing greater accuracy and reliability for its size estimates compared to other giant dinosaurs known from fragmentary remains.
An early reconstruction by Gregory S. Paul estimated Argentinosaurus to be between 30 and 35 meters long and weigh between 80 and 100 tons.
A later publication in Current Science proposed a maximum estimate of 45 meters in length and 100 tons in weight.
A volumetric reconstruction displayed at the Carmen Funes Municipal Museum depicts the animal as 39.7 meters long, 7.3 meters high at the shoulders, and weighing 83.2 tons.
The first bone of Argentinosaurus was discovered in 1987 by a farmer near Plaza Huincul, Argentina.
Guillermo Heredia discovered the first bone, now identified as a fibula, in 1987 on his farm 8 km east of Plaza Huincul in Neuquén Province.
Argentinosaurus used its long neck to reach high trees like Araucaria or to browse low-lying vegetation such as ferns and shrubs on the ground.
Inside its stomach, Argentinosaurus likely ground and crushed vegetation using smooth stones known as gastroliths, as it did not chew its food.
In 2016, Mark Hallett and Matthew Wedel estimated that Argentinosaurus eggs were likely only 1 liter in volume.
Hallett and Wedel estimated that a newly hatched Argentinosaurus was no longer than 1 meter and weighed no more than 5 kilograms.
It is believed that only a very small number of baby Argentinosaurus would survive to reach adulthood.
Argentinosaurus likely traveled in herds of just over a dozen individuals, including juveniles.
Argentinosaurus may have been preyed upon by Mapusaurus, one of the largest known theropods.
Mapusaurus fossils found together suggest it may have hunted in packs to take down large prey like Argentinosaurus.
Argentinosaurus is classified as a member of Titanosauria, the dominant sauropod group during the Cretaceous.
Bonaparte and Coria proposed the family Andesauridae for Argentinosaurus, Andesaurus, and Epachthosaurus.
Argentinosaurus lived during the Early Cretaceous period, specifically the Albian stage.
Argentinosaurus lived in what is now South America.
The Huincul Formation consists of yellowish and greenish fine-to-medium grain sandstones, some containing volcanic ash.
The deposits containing Argentinosaurus were laid down during the Lower Cretaceous period.
Fossilized pollen indicates a wide variety of plants, including ferns, gymnosperms, and angiosperms, lived in the Huincul Formation environment.
Other sauropods found in the same formation include the titanosaur Choconsaurus and rebbachisaurids like Cathartesaura and Limaysaurus.
Theropods discovered in the same formation include Mapusaurus, Skorpiovenator, Huinculsaurus, Overoraptor, Aoniraptor, and Gualicho.
There is an ongoing debate among scientists regarding whether Argentinosaurus was the largest known titanosaur.
One vertebra has been interpreted as the first, fifth, or third vertebra in different studies.
Intermediate estimates suggest Argentinosaurus was 33 to 36 meters long and weighed 70 to 80 tonnes.
Various studies have estimated Argentinosaurus to be between 30 and 39.7 meters long and weigh between 55 and 90 tonnes.
Mazzetta and colleagues used regression equations based on femur anatomy to estimate an average weight of 73 tons, with a possible range of 60 to 88 tons.
In 2008, Jorge Calvo and colleagues revised titanosaur size estimates, calculating Argentinosaurus to be 33 meters long.
In 2023, Paul and Larramendi proposed that the holotype of Argentinosaurus weighed a maximum of 75 to 80 metric tonnes.
